grade_definitions.DISPUTED: Credible sources conflict; do not use as settled fact.
grade_definitions.PROVISIONAL: Thin or single-source evidence; use only with attribution.
grade_definitions.SUPPORTED: Multiple independent or strong sources, but not primary-documentation level.
grade_definitions.UNRESOLVED: Evidence sought but not yet found; flagged for further research.
grade_definitions.VERIFIED: Confirmed by primary or near-primary documentation (contemporary trade press, official records, scholarly monographs with cited primary sources).

claims.text: WVON debuted April 1, 1963 on 1450 AM.
evidence: Searcy 2012: broadcast began at midnight of April 1, 1963
claims.notes: Launch date is among the best-documented facts in the station's history.

claims.text: The WVON call letters stood for 'Voice of the Negro.'
evidence: Chicago Tribune pre-launch note quoted in Searcy 2012
claims.notes: Documented in official records, scholarship, and 2024 owner testimony.

claims.text: Leonard and Phil Chess acquired WHFC (1450 AM) and converted it to WVON.
claims.notes: Exact acquisition date disputed (see U01); the Chess acquisition itself is certain.

claims.text: On February 5, 1975, WVON moved from 1450 to the former WNUS 1390 signal at 5,000 watts.
evidence: Searcy 2012: Globetrotter's first order of business was the 1450-to-1390 move to improve Chicago coverage
claims.notes: Move enlarged coverage; 1450 went dormant.

claims.text: Gannett ended WVON on 1390 in 1983 and simulcast WGCI-FM on the frequency, dropping the WVON calls.
evidence: Searcy 2012: 'Gannett ended WVON in 1983 and began simulcasting the FM broadcast on the 1390 AM frequency'
HR0201: calls changed from WVON to WGCI in 1983
claims.notes: The 1983 loss of the calls is the hinge that makes the Midway reclamation story intelligible.

claims.text: Midway Broadcasting reclaimed the WVON call letters on March 28, 1984.
evidence: Searcy 2012: Midway 'acquired the former WVON call letters when Gannet dropped them in 1984'
claims.notes: Some oral-history accounts say 1983; the FCC-compatible date is March 28, 1984. The distinction is documented, not papered over.

claims.text: WVON switched to an all-talk format in March 1986.
evidence: Salim Muwakkil, In These Times, March 15-21, 1989 (quoting GM Hoyett Owens: changed to talk in March 1986)
Illinois HR0201 (2013): Wesley South opted to change format to talk in 1986
Searcy 2012: 'in 1986, became a talk radio station'
claims.notes: This date is load-bearing: it falsifies the claim that an all-talk WVON powered Harold Washington's 1983 first campaign (see D01).

claims.text: On September 18, 2006, WVON's calls and programming moved to 1690 AM under a local marketing agreement; Midway programs the station while Clear Channel (now iHeartMedia) owns the licensed facility.
evidence: Target Market News (2006) via trade trail
claims.notes: Ownership language must distinguish licensee/owner (iHeartMedia) from operator/programmer (Midway). Do not simplify to 'Midway owns 1690.'

claims.text: The 1690 facility (Facility ID 87178) is licensed to Berwyn, Illinois, Class B, 10,000 watts daytime / 1,000 watts nighttime.
evidence: FCC technical summaries via trade/registry trail
claims.notes: Not independently confirmed against current FCC LMS in this research pass; flagged for verification at publication (see U04).

claims.text: After the April 4, 1968 assassination of Martin Luther King Jr., WVON switched to 24-hour coverage: it sent Roy Wood to Atlanta for on-scene funeral coverage, abandoned its standard format for several days (King speeches, gospel music, news bulletins), aired messages from its entire DJ roster, and encouraged listeners to keep car headlights burning in King's honor.
evidence: First-person accounts of E. Rodney Jones, Lucky Cordell, Pervis Spann (Smithsonian interviews); Herb Kent (Pioneers of Black Radio)
claims.notes: Among the strongest primary-anchored findings in the brief.

claims.text: Melody Spann Cooper became WVON president/general manager in 1994 and chair of Midway Broadcasting in 1999; she describes Midway as Chicago's only Black- and female-owned broadcasting company.
evidence: Spann Cooper testimony, U.S. House Energy and Commerce Subcommittee, April 30, 2024 (primary: owner testimony)
claims.notes: Owner testimony; the 'only' superlative is her claim, reported with attribution.

claims.text: As of 2024 testimony, Midway Broadcasting operates WVON 1690 ('The Talk of Chicago,' urban-talk format), WRLL 1450 ('La Voz de la Comunidad Latina'), and VON-TV.
claims.notes: Current status phrased as documented in 2024/2025, not assumed for 2026.

claims.text: Midway's WXOL launched on 1450 AM in 1979 with a blues-oriented format under a shared-time arrangement with Migala Communications (WCEV).
evidence: Searcy 2012: 'Naming the station WXOL and beginning to broadcast on a part-time basis in 1979'
claims.notes: Shared-time, part-time character matters: this was not an immediate full restoration of the old WVON.

claims.text: After Leonard Chess's 1969 death, the Chess family sold WVON to Globetrotter Communications (George N. Gillett Jr. and Potter Palmer) in a 1970 transaction reported at $9 million.
Combined Communications acquired Globetrotter in 1977; Combined merged with Gannett in 1978, putting WVON under Gannett.
evidence: HR0201: 'in 1977, Globetrotter Communications sold WVON to the Gannett Company'
claims.notes: HR0201 compresses the Combined step; the two-step version is the standard industry account.

claims.text: Berry Gordy sent WVON his new Motown releases first to test their appeal with Black listeners before national release.
evidence: Searcy 2012, p. 233-234: 'Berry Gordy made sure to get all of his records to WVON first in order to test their appeal with African American listeners' (citing the documentary The Dawn of Urban Radio)
Illinois HR0201 (2013): 'special arrangement... every song he produced would be sent immediately to WVON before any other station'
claims.notes: Scholarly-sourced via a documentary film; not independently audited from Motown business records. Use with the citation chain visible.

claims.text: Wesley South hosted 'Hotline,' an hourlong nighttime talk show presenting in-depth coverage of issues facing Black Chicago, focused substantially on civil rights.
evidence: Searcy 2012, p. 134: 'presented a more in depth look at the current issues to Chicago's Black community'
Barlow 1999, p. 211 (via Ramsay): South 'more than anyone was responsible for giving Martin Luther King Jr. a platform on WVON'
claims.notes: Attribution chain runs through the DePaul synthesis; Barlow's monograph is the authority.

claims.text: Pervis Spann used WVON as a vehicle for civil-rights organizing: raising money and recruiting volunteers for the 1964 Mississippi Freedom Summer project, and leading a delegation of Chicago mourners to the funerals of the murdered civil-rights workers.
evidence: Searcy 2012, p. 132 (Spann: 'when there was a march in Virginia, Mississippi or Alabama, wherever... we were there')
claims.notes: Attribution chain: Ramsay cites Barlow; seek Barlow directly for terminal confirmation in a later pass.

claims.text: Reverend Jesse Jackson began his mid-1960s consumer-boycott activism in part through WVON, urging Black listeners to boycott Chicago white-owned businesses that would not hire Black workers.
claims.notes: Dissertation-level evidence; strong but single-author.

claims.text: During the April 1968 unrest, Black Chicagoans called WVON rather than the Chicago police to report current and potential riot activity.
evidence: Searcy 2012, p. 160, citing Herb Kent, An Evening With the Legendary Pioneers of Black Radio: 'One woman called in to tell us about a house full of stuff for Molotov cocktails. She was trusting us, someone she probably had never seen.'
claims.notes: First-person broadcaster account preserved in scholarship; illustrates the station's trusted-node function.

claims.text: WVON disc jockeys went into West and South Side neighborhoods during the 1968 unrest to talk with grieving listeners and urge calm.
evidence: Searcy 2012, p. 160: Pervis Spann ('I would go in and talk with folks'), Lucky Cordell ('We just tried to calm the people down and stop the West side rioting')
claims.notes: First-person accounts; Cordell is candid that looters could not be reached but 'people on the borderline' may have been.

claims.text: Lu Palmer's 'We Shall See in '83' slogan and commentary on WVON helped mobilize Black Chicago for Harold Washington's first mayoral campaign — while the station was still a music-plus-information station, not all-talk.
evidence: Muwakkil, In These Times, March 15-21, 1989: Lu Palmer says occasional information segments helped mobilize the community for Washington's first campaign
Congressional Record Vol. 159 No. 52 (2013): 'Lou spearheaded the election of Harold Washington as Chicago's first Black mayor with the slogan, We Shall See in '83''
claims.notes: The timeline-compatible framing (see D01): influence is real, the all-talk framing is not.

claims.text: After the March 1986 switch to all-talk, WVON's environment aided Harold Washington's 1987 reelection; Lu Palmer said the station went 'beyond and above' for Washington's cause in 1987.
claims.notes: First-person claim from the participant; reported with attribution.

claims.text: By 1989, mainstream journalists, police departments, marketers, and demographers routinely monitored WVON's call-in programs to understand the range of Black Chicago opinion.
evidence: Muwakkil 1989: WTTW's Bruce Dumont taped WVON segments; 'A lot of news organizations monitored our program' (WWRL producer Elisa Keys, on black talk generally); Dumont: 'It's very much like a black town meeting'
claims.notes: Stronger than generic 'voice of the community' rhetoric: documented external monitoring of the forum.

claims.text: Barack Obama, as a state senator, repeatedly guest-hosted Cliff Kelley's WVON show when Kelley was on vacation.
evidence: Congressional Record Vol. 165 No. 46 (2019), Sen. Duckworth tribute: 'guest hosted his show quite a few times when Cliff went on vacation'
claims.notes: The 2019 tribute is commemorative; the Reich timeline gives the 2002 date. Treat year as supported, not verified.

claims.text: Journalist Roland Martin hosted WVON's morning drive-time talk show from 2005 to 2008.
evidence: Editor & Publisher (2007): 'he will continue hosting the morning drive-time talk show on WVON-AM'
Adweek profile: 'Hosted radio talk show in Chicago from 2005 to 2008'

claims.text: Yvonne Daniels joined WVON as morning-drive host in 1982; she had been the first female air personality hired by WLS (1973) and held its overnight shift for nearly eight years.
evidence: Aircheck archivist descriptions (Ellis B. Feaster channel; airchexx.com)
Museum of Broadcast Communications 'Rock Radio Revisited' event listing
claims.notes: The 'first female at WLS' claim rests on archivist/community sources; flag as supported rather than verified.

claims.text: In July 2020, morning hosts Todd Stroger and Maze Jackson left WVON for WBGX after station management told them they could no longer discuss Mayor Lori Lightfoot and to disconnect callers critical of her.
evidence: Robert Feder, Daily Herald, July 7, 2020: 'Maze Jackson, Todd Stroger quit morning show at WVON'
claims.notes: Reported by a veteran Chicago media columnist; WVON management's side not independently obtained in this pass.

claims.text: Bernadine C. Washington was on WVON's original roster; her show 'On the Scene with Bernadine' mixed fashion and shopping guidance with local political news, and she built the 'Bern Club' women's fan organization.
evidence: Searcy 2012: hired by Leonard Chess as a Bronzeville socialite and 'distinguished fashion consultant' to reach female listeners
claims.notes: Corrects the all-male 'Good Guys' memory: women were present from launch, on air and (later) in management.

claims.text: Isabel Joseph Johnson (spelled 'Isabelle' in the HistoryMakers archive) was a member of the Good Guys roster.
evidence: HistoryMakers Digital Library photograph 'WVON Radio Station Team on Stage' (1960s, Lucky Cordell, creator)
claims.notes: Spelling varies by source; flagged in red-team.

claims.text: Under Chess ownership, WVON maintained an all-Black on-air staff and a Black program director, while ownership and top management remained white.
evidence: Searcy 2012: 'groundbreaking because it maintained an all-black broadcasting staff and a black program director... Yet... he adamantly employed white [management]
claims.notes: Important structural nuance: Black voices, white ownership — the pattern Midway later reversed.

claims.text: WVON ranked consistently in the top 5 of most-listened-to stations in the Chicago market during the Good Guys era.
claims.notes: Repeated official/commemorative claim; primary Arbitron/Nielsen books not consulted. Do not upgrade to 'top 3' without ratings data.

claims.text: In 2024 owner testimony, WVON's current information functions included: estate-planning education (attorney Ted London), Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas's weekly segment (credited by the owner with helping return over $300 million in overpaid property taxes), and hosting Rep. Robin Kelly on maternal-mortality legislation.
evidence: Spann Cooper testimony, April 30, 2024 (primary: owner testimony)
claims.notes: Owner testimony, not independently audited outcomes. Report as attributed claims.

claims.text: WVON functions as emergency information infrastructure: warming/relief-center information, weather alerts, and EAS/IPAWS participation.
claims.notes: Attributable to owner testimony; do not overclaim station-specific technical resilience (generator capacity etc.) without documentation.

claims.text: WRLL 1450 ('La Voz de la Comunidad Latina') is Chicago's home for Latino independent broadcasters, operated by Midway.
claims.notes: Shows Midway's multi-community information-ecosystem role beyond WVON.

claims.text: In 2007 WVON's studios moved from 3350 S. Kedzie to the former Soft Sheen Products building at 1000 East 87th Street in Chatham.
evidence: Final Call, March 10, 2011: 'The studio is located at 1000 East 87th Street in Chicago'
claims.notes: The Soft Sheen building was itself Black-owned — the move carried symbolic weight.

claims.text: Cliff Kelley — former 20th Ward alderman (16 years), Englewood High School graduate — hosted on WVON for over 25 years and was known as the 'Governor of Talk Radio.'
HR0201 describes the 1986 format change as giving Chicago 'its first black-talk radio format.'
claims.notes: Official claim; comparative verification against other markets/formats not performed — keep the resolution's framing, not a universal superlative.

claims.text: WHFC (pre-WVON) operated at 1,000 watts daytime / 250 watts nighttime and carried 24 hours per week of African American programming by 1959.
claims.notes: Documents the prehistory: WVON inherited a small facility already serving Black listeners.

claims.text: With Midway's 1984 reclamation of the calls, the station glossed WVON as 'Voice of the Nation.'
evidence: Searcy 2012: 'station transformed its call letters to Voice of the Nation'
claims.notes: The rebranding belongs to the Midway/talk era, not the Chess era.

claims.text: Documented 2025 weekday lineup included Matt McGill, Rufus Williams, Cleopatra Draper, Perri Small, Salim Muwakkil, and Santita Jackson.
evidence: wvon.com (accessed 2026-09-28): podcasts from Matt McGill, Cleopatra Draper, Rufus Williams
claims.notes: Phrased as documented-in-2025; not asserted for 2026.

claims.text: WVON served as a music-marketing outlet for Chess Records and the national R&B/soul industry while simultaneously functioning as a media force fostering collective thought and action among Black Chicagoans.
claims.notes: The dissertation's central thesis; the brief's functional analysis follows it.

claims.text: The 1690 move expanded WVON's daytime signal to 10,000 watts, strengthening its reach relative to the 1450 facility.
claims.notes: Do not present coverage maps as listenership without ratings data.

claims.text: Rev. Jesse Jackson called into WVON to report the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr.
evidence: Congressional Record Vol. 165 No. 46 (2019), Duckworth tribute
claims.notes: Appears only in commemorative tributes; absent from Searcy's documented account of the assassination coverage. Do not state as fact without a contemporary source.

claims.text: WVON disc jockeys rode through neighborhoods with loudspeakers on trucks urging calm after King's assassination.
evidence: Congressional Record Vol. 165 No. 46 (2019), Duckworth tribute
claims.notes: Tribute-only detail; Searcy documents DJs going into the community on foot/in person but no trucks. Quarantine as lore unless corroborated.

claims.text: Martin Luther King Jr. used WVON as his 'bully pulpit' for housing and jobs organizing.
claims.notes: The milder 'platform' version is supported via Barlow (S02). The 'bully pulpit' superlative is tribute rhetoric.

claims.text: WVON was 'the first station specifically designed for Black Chicago' / 'the first Black-talk format' in an absolute sense.
claims.notes: Comparative claims require market-wide verification (WYNR, WAAF, WSBC, WBEE all served Black audiences). Keep qualified.

claims.text: The 1690 transmitter site is at 86th and Kedzie in Chicago.
claims.notes: wvon.com history cited 87th & Kedzie in some versions; studios confirmed at 1000 E. 87th St. Treat tower location as provisional pending FCC ASR/site data.

claims.text: WHFC's 97.9 FM simulcast WVON's programming until 1965, when it became jazz-formatted WSDM.
claims.notes: FM-side history not verified against primary sources in this pass.

claims.text: WVON's all-talk format powered Harold Washington's 1983 first mayoral campaign.
evidence: Against: Muwakkil 1989 (talk began March 1986); Searcy 2012; HR0201 (1986)
For: loose commemorative phrasing in some tributes
claims.notes: FALSE as stated. Timeline-compatible framing: in 1983 WVON was music-plus-information/commentary and Lu Palmer promoted Washington with 'We Shall See in '83'; the all-talk format aided the 1987 reelection environment. See CTL-DR-BMI-002 red-team.

claims.text: Pervis Spann and Wesley South purchased WVON on April 1, 1963.
evidence: For: 2022 Congressional Pervis Spann tribute (single sentence)
Against: all ownership records (Chess 1963; Globetrotter 1970; Gannett 1978; Midway 1984)
claims.notes: The tribute sentence is simply wrong; Spann and South acquired the calls in 1984 via Midway. Do not repeat.

claims.text: Midway Broadcasting was founded in 1979.
evidence: Against: Searcy 2012: Spann and South 'in 1977... partnered to form the Midway Broadcasting Company' with WXOL broadcasting from 1979
claims.notes: Company formation vs. on-air launch may explain the gap; exact founding year unresolved. Present both with attribution.

claims.text: Exact date of the Chess acquisition of WHFC: spring 1962 (Searcy) vs. early 1963 (Broadcasting, Feb 18, 1963).
evidence: Searcy 2012: 'In the spring of 1962, Leonard Chess purchased WHFC 1450 AM'
claims.notes: Announcement vs. closing vs. planning dates may all be in play. FCC history cards would resolve; flagged for CTL-DR-MEDIA-001.

claims.text: Whether Jesse Jackson called WVON with news of King's assassination (see P01).
claims.notes: Needs a contemporary (April 1968) source: Defender/Tribune/Billboard archives.

claims.text: First documented public use of 'Voice of the Nation' as the calls' gloss.
evidence: Searcy 2012 places it with the 1984 reclamation
claims.notes: Trade-press or station-imaging sources from 1984-1986 would pin this down.

claims.text: Current FCC LMS technical and ownership records for Facility ID 87178 (1690).
claims.notes: fccdata.org was not extractable in this pass; direct LMS confirmation recommended at publication.

claims.text: WVON's status, lineup, and ownership arrangement as of 2026.
claims.notes: Do not assert 2026 facts without fresh confirmation.

claims.text: Rank-and-file staff histories: news staff, producers, engineers, sales and community-affairs personnel across eras.
claims.notes: The record is personality-heavy; systematic staff recovery is deferred to CTL-DR-MEDIA-001.
